Despite substantial advances in data availability, an operational gap remains: can mesohabitat types be predicted directly from satellite features across streamflow regimes without reliance on site-specific LiDAR or dense field annotation, and evaluated using temporally independent, hydrologically relevant validation? Object-based pipelines often require site/timestep retuning and can degrade under heterogeneous riverscape conditions (i.e. specular reflection, shadows, turbidity), limiting transferability in dynamic fluvial environments (Demarchi et al., 2016, 2016; Kutz et al., 2022; Zhang et al., 2023).
Deep learning and modern ML offer stronger representation capacity but remain sensitive to label scarcity, class imbalance, and domain shift across color/turbidity/illumination (
Aggarwal, 2018; Fix and Hodges, 1989; Ma et al., 2019; Maskey et al., 2018; Vahidi et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2019; Wurm et al., 2019).

Moreover, ecohydraulic mapping at scale is constrained by the cost and data demands of LiDAR-driven or fully calibrated hydraulic models (Lindenschmidt and Carr, 2018; Schwartz, 2016). Because mesohabitat composition shifts with streamflow, models must respect flow dependence and test temporal generalization (Aadland, 1993; Harris et al., 2024). These considerations motivate a label-efficient, imagery-first strategy that exploits high-cadence VHR sources (e.g., PlanetScope) for multi-date coverage while limiting mixed-pixel issues typical of coarser sensors in narrow channel widths (e.g. Planet Labs PBC, 2024; USGS, 2023c).
